prompt: Where does a screen reader get what it says about a button?

choices.text: From recognising the icon's shape in the pixels
choices.why: It does not look at pixels; a green tick means nothing to it.

choices.text: From the app's store description
choices.why: The store listing is not read element by element on the screen.

choices.text: From what the app declared about the element
choices.why: Right. Label, role, state and hint all come from declarations, made by the component or by you.

choices.text: From the app's source code, read when it is installed
choices.why: The screen reader asks the running app about each element, not its source.

prompt: Put the parts a screen reader speaks for one element in the order they come.
With TalkBack on, how does a user reach the next element and then activate it?

choices.text: Swipes right, then double-taps anywhere
choices.why: Right. Android's testing documentation describes exactly this: the swipe moves focus, and only the double tap activates.

choices.text: Shakes the phone, then presses a volume button
choices.why: Neither is how linear navigation works.

choices.text: Taps the element directly, as a sighted user would
choices.why: A single tap moves the focus or reads; it does not activate.

choices.text: Long-presses until the element is spoken twice
choices.why: Not a gesture the documentation describes for moving or activating.

prompt: A week of 7 sessions, each row heard as 4 separate elements. How many swipes does it take to pass every row?
A planner button turns from grey to green when tapped, and declares nothing else. What does a VoiceOver user learn from tapping it?

choices.text: The hint, which every button speaks after a tap
choices.why: A hint exists only if the app set one, and it says what will happen, not what did.

choices.text: That it is now green
choices.why: The screen reader does not read colours from pixels.

choices.text: That it is now checked, inferred from the change
choices.why: Nothing is inferred; state comes from a declaration.

choices.text: Nothing: no state was declared
choices.why: Right. The colour change is visual only; without a declared state, the screen reader has nothing to say.

prompt: Which label is the best one for the planner's tick on the SQL session of Friday?

choices.text: Green tick icon at the right of the session row
choices.why: It describes the look, which the user cannot see, and not what happens.

choices.text: SQL, Friday 23 October, 60 minutes
choices.why: Right. It names only this session, and the checkbox role and state say the rest.

choices.text: Mark done button
choices.why: The role already says button; the user hears it twice, and seven rows sound the same.

choices.text: Tick
choices.why: Every row would say the same word, and it names a shape.

prompt: Match each platform's way of making a row one element for the screen reader.
Why does a Compose `Text` need no `contentDescription`?

choices.text: Because Compose hides text from screen readers
choices.why: The opposite: the text is what gets read.

choices.text: The screen reader announces the text itself
choices.why: Right. Android's documentation says exactly that; a label is only for things that show pictures instead of words.

choices.text: Because Text is not focusable
choices.why: It is read in the list like any element; it needs no extra label.

choices.text: Because labels exist only on iOS
choices.why: Android's label is contentDescription.

prompt: Which of these should be hidden from the screen reader? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: a decorative drawing beside the week's total
choices.why: It adds no information and costs a swipe.

choices.text: the week's total
choices.why: That is the screen's main information.

choices.text: the tick on each session
choices.why: It is the control; it needs a label, role and state, not hiding.

choices.text: a divider line between sessions
choices.why: Pure decoration, like the drawing.

prompt: A team puts the only explanation of a swipe-to-delete gesture in an `accessibilityHint`. What goes wrong?

choices.text: Hints are refused by React Native on Android
choices.why: The property exists; the problem is who hears it.

choices.text: The hint is read before the label and confuses users
choices.why: It comes after the label, after a pause.

choices.text: Nothing goes wrong; hints are always spoken
choices.why: React Native's documentation says VoiceOver reads them only when hints are turned on.

choices.text: Users who turned hints off never hear it
choices.why: Right. Nothing essential belongs in a hint alone; offer the action as a control too.

prompt: Match each source to the minimum target it gives.
The planner's tick is drawn at 24 × 24 dp. How many dp of padding does it need on each side to reach Android's minimum?
How does the lesson fix the tick that is too small to tap?

choices.text: Pads the target and leaves the drawing at 24
choices.why: Right. The target and the drawing are separate numbers, and only the target must reach the minimum.

choices.text: Draws the tick at 48 so the drawing and target match
choices.why: That works, but changes the design; the lesson keeps the drawing at 24.

choices.text: Removes the tick and makes the whole app larger
choices.why: Nothing that drastic is needed.

choices.text: Adds a hint telling users to tap carefully
choices.why: A hint does not make anything easier to hit.

prompt: A toolbar holds five 24-point icons, side by side with no gap. Each is padded to 44. What new problem appears?

choices.text: None: padding never has a cost, since nothing is drawn larger
choices.why: It costs space, and here the spaces collide.

choices.text: The icons become blurry
choices.why: The drawing does not change size at all.

choices.text: The grown targets overlap
choices.why: Right. Every target grew into its neighbour; that is where fewer toolbar items becomes an accessibility rule.

choices.text: The screen reader reads the padding as a separate element
choices.why: Padding is part of the same element's target.

prompt: The HIG lists 44 × 44 pt and 28 × 28 pt for iOS controls. How do the two relate?

choices.text: 44 is the default; 28 the smallest listed
choices.why: Right. The planner aims for 44 on iOS.

choices.text: 28 is for iPhone and 44 for iPad
choices.why: Both numbers are given for iOS and iPadOS together.

choices.text: 44 is in pixels and 28 in points, so they are equal
choices.why: Both are in points.

choices.text: 28 is the new minimum and replaces 44
choices.why: The page gives both, as default and minimum.

prompt: What contrast ratio does contrast.ts report for #8A8A8A on white? Give two decimals.
What contrast ratio does WCAG 2.2 ask of ordinary text against its background?

choices.why: That is for large text and for the edges of controls.
That is a stricter level than the AA minimum the platforms point at.
Right. Criterion 1.4.3, level AA.
No criterion uses 3.5; the two numbers are 4.5 for text and 3 for large text.

prompt: The contrast ratio is (lighter + 0.05) divided by (darker + 0.05), where each colour enters as its relative ___.
contrast.ts reports 4.48:1 for #777777 on white. Why does the lesson not accept it?

choices.text: Because #777777 is not a brand colour
choices.why: Any grey can become the brand's; the number is the problem.

choices.text: 4.48 is below 4.5, however close
choices.why: Right. A threshold must be met, not nearly met; rounded it would look like a pass, which is why the program prints two decimals.

choices.text: Because the dark theme fails too
choices.why: The dark pair passes at 5.41.

choices.text: Because greys never pass on white
choices.why: #767676 passes, one step darker.

prompt: Why did fixing `muted` in tokens.ts fix both the Material and the iOS theme at once?

choices.text: Because contrast.ts rewrites both theme files
choices.why: contrast.ts only reads and reports.

choices.text: Because the HIG and Material share one palette
choices.why: They name colours differently; the planner's tokens are what is shared.

choices.text: iOS copies Android's colours at build time
choices.why: No such copy exists; both read one file.

choices.text: Both themes are built from the same token
choices.why: Right. onSurfaceVariant and secondaryLabel both read brand.light.muted, so one edit reaches every theme.

prompt: Up to what size does WCAG's Resize Text criterion ask that text can be enlarged without loss?

choices.text: 120 percent
choices.why: Far short of the criterion.

choices.text: 150 percent
choices.why: Short of the criterion.

choices.text: 200 percent
choices.why: Right. The HIG asks for at least the same on the phone.

choices.text: 400 percent
choices.why: More than the criterion asks, though iOS's own range reaches past 300.

prompt: At the largest accessibility size the planner's row is cut off. Which change follows the HIG's advice?

choices.text: Stack the lines and let the row grow
choices.why: Right. A stacked layout, and a row as tall as its content: nothing is cut.

choices.text: Fix the text at 17 points so it never grows
choices.why: That defeats Dynamic Type for the people who need it.

choices.text: Shorten every course name to three letters
choices.why: That is truncation by hand, and the HIG asks to keep it to a minimum.

choices.text: Hide the date and the minutes at the accessibility sizes
choices.why: That loses content, which is what the criterion forbids.

prompt: With Reduce Motion on, what should the planner's mark-done animation keep?

choices.text: The bounce, slowed down
choices.why: A bounce is decoration, and slow motion is still motion.

choices.text: Nothing at all; the row should disappear
choices.why: The row is information; it stays.

choices.text: The flight off screen, without the bounce
choices.why: The flight is the decoration that goes.

choices.text: The tick filling in
choices.why: Right. The information always stays; only the decoration goes.

prompt: A green 'done' row and a red 'overdue' row both pass 4.5:1 against white. Why is that not enough?

choices.text: Because red always fails the contrast check on a white background
choices.why: Both pass, by the question's own numbers.

choices.text: Colour is the only signal, and some cannot tell them apart
choices.why: Right. Under WCAG 1.4.1 colour must never be the only signal: add a shape, a word, a decoration.

choices.text: Because contrast is measured only in dark mode
choices.why: It is measured in each appearance.

choices.text: Because 4.5:1 applies only to large text
choices.why: 4.5 is for ordinary text; large text needs 3.

prompt: Which signals tell a user that a planner session is done? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: the tick is filled
choices.why: A shape, visible without colour.

choices.text: the minutes are struck through
choices.why: A text decoration, also visible without colour.

choices.text: the screen reader says checked
choices.why: The declared state, for users who cannot see.

choices.text: the row plays a sound
choices.why: The planner adds no sound; the lesson lists three visual signals and the declared state.

prompt: On iOS, the system setting that grows text in every app that uses text styles is called Dynamic ___.
